title: What a sehaj path is
hook: everyone binged the series in a weekend; you're a month in and three episodes deep
tomorrow: a page a day: how long until you reach the end?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hukamnama: one hymn nobody picks, the top of the left-hand page, today's order. One page a day. Which raises a bigger idea: what if the pages kept going?
screen: `TODAY'S ORDER: ONE PAGE.` → `WHAT IF THE PAGES KEPT GOING?`

segments.voice: Everyone at school binged the whole series in one weekend. You're a month in, three episodes deep, and somebody spoils the ending. Some things aren't meant to be raced. Yesterday's question was: what if you read the whole Granth, slowly, your own way? There's a name for that. It's one of the ordinary ways Sikhs read the Granth from its first page to its last, in a home, in a family, around school and shifts and dinner. It's called a sehaj path.
screen: `BINGED IN A WEEKEND.` → `SOME THINGS AREN'T RACED.` → `A SEHAJ PATH.`

segments.voice: Path means a reading. Sehaj, sahaj in the Granth, is a word the Gurus use for ease, a steady, natural poise. The Anand opens with it. Guru Amar Das sings, in paraphrase: I have found the True Guru, found him with sahaj, with ease, and my mind rings with celebration. So a sehaj path is the whole Granth read with that ease. A page, or a few, whenever the day allows, by one person or by a family taking turns. Compare its sibling, the akhand path: a reading without a break, start to finish, readers handing off in shifts so the voice never stops. Both are honored. They just ask different things. The akhand path asks for stamina. The sehaj path asks for faithfulness, a little and often, over a long stretch of ordinary life. That's what it gives a busy week. There's no deadline to fail. A week of exams, a hospital visit, a move, and the reading waits; you open it again where you left off. Here's what to tell a friend: one of the ways Sikhs read their entire scripture is built around the fact that life gets busy. Ease isn't a shortcut here. It's the name of the practice.
screen: `SAHAJ: EASE, NATURAL POISE.` · `THE WHOLE GRANTH, A LITTLE AT A TIME.` · `AKHAND: NONSTOP. SEHAJ: STEADY.` · `NO DEADLINE TO FAIL.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN PACE.`

segments.voice: Sit the way you'd sit to read for a long while: feet on the floor, back easy, shoulders loose, hands open in your lap. Let your breath find its own pace without pushing it faster or slower. When it has settled, say out loud the pace that would fit your real life, a page, a few lines, a hymn, and let that be enough.
Sehaj path: a reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib at your own pace, with ease, a little at a time, by one person or a family. The fourteenth word of the year.
Your line: your own pace. In a sehaj path, steady counts for more than fast. Fourteen, and no rush.

howItsDone: Sikh families and individuals read the whole Guru Granth Sahib in a sehaj path at their own pace, often a little each day, and close it with a bhog; an akhand path is the unbroken reading by readers in turn.
